words.definition: Lasting for a short period of time.
words.origin: From New Latin ephemerus, from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros), the more common form of ἐφημέριος (ephēmérios, “of, for, or during the day, living or lasting but for a day, short-lived, temporary”), from ἐπί (epí, “on”) + ἡμέρα (hēméra,…

words.definition: Implied, but not made explicit, especially through silence.
words.origin: Borrowed from late Middle French tacite, or from Latin tacitus (“that is passed over in silence, done without words, assumed as a matter of course, silent”), from tacere (“to be silent”).

words.definition: Done only or merely to conform to a minimal standard or to fulfill a protocol or presumptive duty.
words.origin: From Late Latin perfunctōrius (“careless, negligent”), from the past participial stem of perfungor, perfunct- (“perform, carry through”), from per- + fungor.

words.definition: Being everywhere at once: omnipresent.
words.origin: From ubiquity + -ous, from Medieval Latin ubīquitās, from Latin ubīque (“everywhere”), from ubī̆ (“where”) + -que (“each, ever”). Compare ubiety.

words.definition: Practical, concerned with making decisions and actions that are useful in practice, not just theory.
words.origin: From Middle French pragmatique, from Late Latin pragmaticus (“relating to civil affair; in Latin, as a noun, a person versed in the law who furnished arguments and points to advocates and orators, a kind of attorney”), from Ancient Greek…

words.definition: A minor distinction.
words.origin: Borrowed from French nuance (“nuance, shade, hue”). Omitting several steps, from Latin nūbēs. Compare typologically Italian sfumatura (< Latin fūmus).

words.definition: British and Canada standard spelling of candor.
Simultaneously experiencing or expressing opposing or contradictory feelings, beliefs, motivations, or meanings.
words.origin: Back-formation from ambivalence, from German Ambivalenz, from Latin ambi- (“in two ways”) + valeō (“be strong”); equivalent to ambi- + -valent. Compare ambivert.

words.definition: Compressed into a small area; compact.

words.definition: Containing or using more words than necessary; long-winded, wordy.
words.origin: From Latin verbōsus (“prolix, wordy, verbose”). Verbōsus is derived from verbum (“word”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *werh₁- (“to say, speak”)) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of, overly, prone to’ forming adjectives from nouns).

words.definition: Characterized by very precise, conscientious attention to details.
words.origin: Learned borrowing from Latin meticulōsus (“full of fear, timid, fearful, terrible, frightful”), from metus (“fear”) and -culōsus, extracted from perīculōsus (“perilous”).

words.definition: Hasty or superficial.
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French cursoire (“rapid”), from Latin cursorius (“hasty, of a race or running”).

words.definition: Composed of inherently different or distinct elements; incongruous.
words.origin: First attested in 1586; either borrowed from Middle French desparat or directly from Latin disparātus, perfect passive participle of disparō (“to divide”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from dis-…

words.definition: Naturally as part or consequence of something.
words.origin: From Latin inhaerentem, accusative singular of inhaerēns, present active participle of inhaereō (“to be closely connected with; to adhere to”).

words.definition: Innate, inherent, inseparable from the thing itself, essential.
words.origin: From Middle French intrinsèque, from Latin intrīnsecus (“on the inside, inwardly”), from *intrim, an assumed adverbial form of inter (“within”) + secus (“by, on the side”).

words.definition: Seemingly, apparently, on the surface; supposedly, according to representations or implications made by someone (especially when their motives are suspected by others).
words.origin: From ostensible + -ly.

words.definition: Of, resembling, relating to, or consisting of a name or names.
words.origin: From the Middle English nominalle (“of nouns”), borrowed from Latin nōminālis (“of names”), ultimately from oblique stem of Latin nōmen, nōminis (“name”) + -al.

words.definition: Thin in substance or consistency.
words.origin: Irregularly formed from Latin tenuis (“thin, slight”) + -ous. Compare tenuious.

words.definition: Worthy of note; pertinent or relevant.
words.origin: The heraldic sense “leaping” and the sense “projecting outward” are borrowed from Latin salientem, the accusative form of saliēns (“springing, leaping”) (whence -ent), present participle of saliō (“leap, spring”, verb).

words.definition: A right that attaches to land, in Scots law.
words.origin: Inherited from Middle English pertinent, borrowed from Old French pertinent and Latin pertinēns, pertinentem.

words.definition: In excess of what is required or sufficient.
words.origin: From Middle English superfluous, from Latin superfluus (“superfluous”) + -ous, from superfluō (“overflow”), from super (“above, more than, over”) + fluō (“flow”). Compare mellifluous and fluid, also from Latin.

words.definition: Superfluous; exceeding what is necessary (and therefore no longer needed because other things fulfill its task or purpose).
words.origin: From Latin redundāns, present participle of redundō (“to overflow, redound”), from red- (“again, back”) + undō (“to surge, flood”), from unda (“a wave”).

words.definition: On the periphery or boundary.
words.origin: From peripher(y) + -al.

words.definition: Highest, supreme; also, chief, leading, pre-eminent.

words.definition: Able to be neglected, ignored or excluded from consideration; too small or unimportant to be of concern.
words.origin: From negligence/negligent + -ible, as if from New Latin *negligibilis, from Latin neglegō (“to neglect”) + -ibilis (“-ible”).

words.definition: Of the essence or essential element of a thing.
words.origin: From Middle English substantif, from Old French substantif.

words.definition: Open to multiple interpretations.
words.origin: From Latin ambiguus (“moving from side to side, of doubtful nature”), from ambigere (“to go about, wander, doubt”), from ambi- (“around, about, on both sides”) + agere (“to drive, move”).

words.definition: Having two or more equally applicable meanings; capable of double or multiple interpretation.
words.origin: From Late Latin aequivocus + -al, from aequus + vocō. By surface analysis, equi- + vocal.

words.definition: Unambiguous; without equivocation or ambiguity; singularly clear, unmistakable, or unquestionable
words.origin: From un- + equivocal.

words.definition: Very specific, clear, or detailed.
words.origin: Borrowed from French explicite, from Latin explicitus (“disentangled, easy”), variant of explicātus.

words.definition: Suggested indirectly, without being directly expressed; Implied.
words.origin: From Middle French implicite, from Latin implicitus, past participle of implico (“to infold, involve, entangle”); see implicate.

words.definition: Touchable; able to be touched or felt; perceptible by the sense of touch.
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French tangible, from Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tangere (“to touch”)

words.definition: Incapable of being perceived by the senses; incorporeal.
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French intangible, from Medieval Latin intangibilis, from Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tango.

words.definition: Seemingly or apparently valid, likely, or acceptable; conceivably true or likely.
words.origin: From Latin plausibilis (“deserving applause, praiseworthy, acceptable, pleasing”), from the participle stem of plaudere (“to applaud”).

words.definition: False, not authentic, not genuine.
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin spurius (“illegitimate, bastardly”), possibly related to sperno or from Etruscan.

words.definition: Seemingly well-reasoned, plausible or true, but actually fallacious.
words.origin: From Middle English speciose, specious, from Anglo-Norman specious, Middle French specieux, and their etymon Latin speciōsus (“good-looking”).

words.definition: Characterized by fallacy; false or mistaken.
words.origin: From Old French fallacieux (whence -acious), from Latin fallācia, from fallāx, from fallere.

words.definition: Reasonable and convincing; based on evidence.
words.origin: From French cogent, from Latin cōgēns, present active participle of cōgō (“drive together, compel”), from cō + agō (“drive”).

words.definition: Unified; sticking together; making up a whole.
words.origin: From Middle French coherent, from Latin cohaērēns, from co- + haereō. By surface analysis, cohere + -ent.

words.definition: Not making logical sense; not logically connected or consistent.
words.origin: From in- + coherent.

words.definition: Clear; easily understood.

words.definition: Quickly and critically discerning.
words.origin: From Latin astūtus, from astus (“craft”).

words.definition: Showing clever resourcefulness in practical matters.

words.definition: Sagacious in adapting means to ends; circumspect in action, or in determining any line of conduct.
words.origin: Inherited from Middle English prudent, from Old French prudent, from Latin prūdēns, contracted from prōvidēns (“foresight”) (English providence), the present participle of prōvideō (“to forsee; to provide for”). Unrelated to prude.

words.definition: Not prudent; lacking prudence or discretion; indiscreet; injudicious; not paying attention to the consequences of one's actions.
words.origin: From Middle French imprudent, from Latin imprūdens (“not foreseeing, ignorant”), prefix im- (“not”) + prūdens (“foreseeing, skilled, judicious”).

words.definition: Having, characterized by, or done with good judgment or sound thinking.
words.origin: From French judicieux, ultimately derived from Latin iudico. Related to judge, judicial.

words.definition: Based on individual discretion or judgment; not based on any objective distinction, perhaps even made at random.
words.origin: From Middle English arbitrarie, Latin arbitrārius (“arbitrary, uncertain”), from arbiter (“witness, on-looker, listener, judge, overseer”).

words.definition: Impulsive and unpredictable; determined by chance, impulse, or whim.
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French capricieux, from Italian capriccioso, from capriccio. By surface analysis, caprice + -ious.

words.definition: Unsteady, random; prone to unexpected changes; not consistent.
words.origin: From Middle English erratik, from Middle French erratique (from Old French erratique) and its etymon Classical Latin errāticus.

words.definition: Rare and scattered in occurrence.

words.definition: Stopping and starting, occurring, or presenting at intervals; coming after a particular time span.
words.origin: From Middle French intermittent, from Latin intermittens (“sending between”), from prefix inter- (“among, on”) + mittens (“sending”), from mittere (“to send”).

words.definition: Without pause or stop; not ending, especially to the point of annoyance.
words.origin: From Late Middle English incessaunte, from Late Latin incessāns, incessantem, from Latin in- + cessāns.

words.definition: Lasting or remaining active throughout the year, for multiple years, or all the time.
words.origin: The adjective is borrowed from Latin perennis (“lasting through the whole year or for several years, perennial; continual, everlasting, perpetual”) + English -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives).

words.definition: Passing or disappearing with time; transitory.
words.origin: From Late Latin transiēnt- (for classical transeunt-), stem of transiēns, present participle of trānsīre (“to go over, to pass”).

words.definition: Passing quickly; of short duration.
words.origin: From Middle English fleten (“to float”), from Old English flēotan (“to float”), from Proto-Germanic *fleutaną, from Proto-Indo-European *plewd-. By surface analysis, fleet + -ing.

words.definition: To make worse (a problem, bad situation, negative feeling, etc.).

words.definition: To make better, or improve, something perceived to be in a negative condition.
words.origin: Alteration of meliorate after French améliorer.

words.definition: To reduce or lessen the severity of a pain or difficulty.
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin alleviatus, past participle of alleviāre (“to lighten; to alleviate”). By surface analysis, al- + Latin lev- + -i- + -ate.

words.definition: An increase in the severity of something (such as a disease)
words.origin: From Middle English exacerbacyoun, from Latin exacerbātiōnem, from exacerbāre (“to provoke, make harsh”). See exacerbate.

words.definition: To make something happen suddenly and quickly.
words.origin: From Latin praecipitātus, perfect passive participle of praecipitō (“throw down, hurl down, throw headlong”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from praeceps (“head foremost, headlong”) (praecipit- in its oblique stem), from prae…

words.definition: To remove the possibility of; to rule out; to prevent or exclude; to render impossible.
words.origin: Learned borrowing from Latin praeclūdere.

words.definition: to avoid or get around something; to bypass
words.origin: Learned borrowing from Latin circumveniō.

words.definition: To anticipate and prevent or bypass (something which would otherwise have been necessary or required); to render (something) unnecessary.
words.origin: First attested in 1567; borrowed from Latin obviātus, perfect passive participle of obviō (“to block, to hinder”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

words.definition: To dig underneath (something), to make a passage for destructive or military purposes; to sap.
words.origin: From under- + mine.

words.definition: A large cushion or pillow, usually cylindrical in shape.
words.origin: From Middle English bolster, bolstre, from Old English bolster (“pillow”), from Proto-West Germanic *bolstr, from Proto-Germanic *bulstraz (“pillow, cushion”).

words.definition: To confirm or support something with additional evidence; to attest or vouch for.
words.origin: First attested in the 1530s; borrowed from Latin corrōborātus (“strengthened”), perfect passive participle of corrōborō (“to support, corroborate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from con-…

words.definition: To verify something by supplying evidence; to authenticate or corroborate.
words.origin: From Medieval Latin substantiatus (“given substance”), from the verb substantiare, first used 1657.

words.definition: To prove (something) to be false or incorrect.
words.origin: From Latin refūtō (“refute, repudiate”).

words.definition: To drive back or beat back; to repulse.
words.origin: Inherited from Middle English rebutten, rebouten, from Old French reboter, rebuter, rebouter, etc., from re- + boter, buter, bouter (“to butt”). Entered English around 1302-1307.

words.definition: To yield or suffer; to surrender; to grant
words.origin: From Middle English [Term?], from Old French conceder, from Latin concēdō (“give way, yield”), from con- (“wholly”) + cēdō (“to yield, give way, to go, grant”), from Proto-Indo-European *ked- (“to go, yield”).

words.definition: To rest satisfied, or apparently satisfied, or to rest without opposition and discontent (usually implying previous opposition or discontent); to accept or consent by silence or by omitting to object.
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French acquiescer, from Latin acquiescō; ad + quiescō (“to rest”), from quies (“rest”).

words.definition: To delay or postpone.
words.origin: Originally a variant of (and hence a doublet of) differ; from Middle English differren (“to postpone”), from Old French differer, from Latin differō. Doublet of differ and dilate.

words.definition: Great respect.
words.origin: From French déférence. Morphologically defer + -ence.

words.definition: Unwilling to communicate; keeping one's thoughts and opinions to oneself; reserved or restrained.
words.origin: Latin reticēns, present participle of reticeō (“to keep silence”).

words.definition: Impartial and free from prejudice.
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin candidus (“white”).

words.definition: Possessing tact; able to deal with people in a sensitive manner.
words.origin: From tact + -ful.

words.definition: Concerning the relationships between the governments of countries.
words.origin: From French diplomatique and its etymon New Latin diplōmaticus. By surface analysis, diplomat + -ic.

words.definition: Engaged in warfare, warring.
words.origin: From Latin belligerans (“waging war”), present active participle of belligerō (“to wage war”), from belliger (“waging war, warlike”), from bellum (“war”) + -ger (from gerō (“to lead, wage, carry on”)).

words.definition: Willing to conciliate, or to make concessions.
Noble and generous in spirit.
words.origin: From Latin magnanimus, from magnus (“great”) + animus (“soul, mind”). Displaced native Old English miċelmōd (literally “big-minded”).

words.definition: Childishly irritable.
words.origin: From Middle French, from Latin petulāns, akin to petō (“to ask for”).

words.definition: Showing anger or indignation, especially at something unjust or wrong.
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin indignāns, present participle of indignor (“to consider as unworthy, be angry or displeased at”), from in- (“privative”) + dignor (“to deem worthy”), from dignus (“worthy”).

words.definition: Uncritically satisfied with oneself or one's achievements; smug.
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin complacēns (“very pleasing”), present participle of complacēre (“to please at the same time, be very pleasing”), from com- (“together”) + placēre (“to please”); see please and compare complaisant.

words.definition: Lacking self-confidence; timid; modest
words.origin: From Latin diffīdentem, present participle of diffīdere (“to mistrust”). Doublet of defiant.

words.definition: Showing willingness to take bold risks; recklessly daring.
words.origin: From Latin audacia (“boldness”) + -ious, from audax (“bold”), from audeō (“to be bold, to dare”).

words.definition: Clinging to an object or surface; adhesive.
words.origin: From Latin tenāx (“holding fast, clinging”), from tenēre (“to hold”), + -ious.

words.definition: Returning quickly to original shape after force is applied; elastic. (of objects or substances)
words.origin: From Latin resiliēns, resilientem (“rebounding”, present active participle of resiliō) (whence -ent), from saliō (“leap, jump”).

words.definition: Dangerously insecure or unstable; perilous.
words.origin: From Latin precārius (“begged for, obtained by entreaty”), from prex, precis (“prayer”). Compare French précaire, Portuguese precário, and Spanish and Italian precario.

words.definition: Evaporating or vaporizing readily under normal conditions.
words.origin: From Middle French volatile, from Latin volātilis (“flying; swift; temporary; volatile”), from volō (“to fly”).

words.definition: Proponent of stoicism, a school of thought, from in 300 B.C.E. up to about the time of Marcus Aurelius, who holds that by cultivating an understanding of the logos, or natural law, one can be free of suffering.
words.origin: From Latin stōicus (noun via Middle English Stoycis pl), from Ancient Greek Στωϊκός (Stōïkós), from Ποικίλη Στοά (Poikílē Stoá, “the Stoa Poikile”, literally “painted portico”), the portico in Athens where Zeno of Citium was teaching.

words.definition: Engaged in, involving, or reflecting deep or serious thought.
words.origin: From Middle English pensif, pensyfe, pencyve, from Old French pensif (“thoughtful”), from penser (“to think”) (from Latin pēnsō) + -if (English -ive).

words.definition: Full of longing or yearning.
words.origin: Presumably from *whistful, from whist (“silent”) + -ful, based on older wistly. It is implausible that it derives from wishful, the required sound change being wishful → *wisful → wistful, which could not occur in Modern English,…

words.definition: Neat; eloquent; applicable; relevant.
words.origin: From Middle English poynaunt, poynant, borrowed from Anglo-Norman puignant, poynaunt etc., present participle of poindre (“to prick”), from Latin pungō (“prick”). Doublet of pungent.

words.definition: Of or relating to, made up of, or positioned among or within, the viscera (“internal organs of the body, especially those contained within the abdominal and thoracic cavities”).
words.origin: From Middle French viscéral (modern French viscéral), or from its etymon Medieval Latin viscerālis (“internal”) + English -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives).

words.definition: Harmless; producing no ill effect.
words.origin: From Latin innocuus (“harmless”) (therefore, no gemination in + nocuous).

words.definition: Causing harm in a stealthy, often gradual, manner.
words.origin: From Middle French insidieux, from Latin īnsidiōsus (“cunning, artful, deceitful”), from īnsidiae (“a lying in wait, an ambush, artifice, stratagem”) + -ōsus, from īnsideō (“to sit in or on”), from in (“in, on”) + sedeō (“to sit”).

words.definition: Causing much harm in a subtle way.
words.origin: From Middle English, from Old French pernicios, from Latin perniciōsus (“destructive”), from perniciēs (“destruction”), from per (“through”) + nex (“slaughter, death”).

words.definition: Kind; gentle; mild.
words.origin: From Middle English benigne, benygne, from Old French benigne, from Latin benignus (“kind, good”), from bene (“well”) + genus (“origin, kind”). Compare malign.

words.definition: Evil or malignant in disposition, nature, intent or influence.
words.origin: From Middle English maligne, from Old French maligne, from Latin malignus, from malus (“bad”) + genus (“sort, kind”). Compare benign.

words.definition: Conspicuous, exceptional, outstanding; usually in a negative sense.
words.origin: From Latin ēgregius, from e- (“out of”), + grex (“flock”), + English adjective suffix -ous, from Latin suffix -osus (“full of”); reflecting the positive connotations of "standing out from the flock".

words.definition: Obvious and offensive; blatant; scandalous.
words.origin: From Middle French flagrant, from Latin flagrantem, present participle of flagrare (“blaze, burn”). More at black.

words.definition: Obvious, on show; unashamed; loudly obtrusive or offensive.

words.definition: Of an action or movement: very delicate or slight, and thus barely noticeable; not obvious; inconspicuous, unintrusive.

words.definition: Open and not concealed or secret.
words.origin: From Middle English overt, uverte (“open, uncovered; unfastened; accessible, unobstructed; clear, manifest”), from Anglo-Norman overt, Middle French ouvert, Old French overt, ouvert, uvert (“opened”) (modern French ouvert), past participle…

words.definition: Secret, surreptitious, concealed.
words.origin: From Middle English covert, from Old French covert, past participle of covrir (“to cover”) (corresponding to Latin coopertus); cognate to cover. Not closely related to overt, despite what the most common pronunciation would suggest.

words.definition: Existing or present, but concealed or inactive.
words.origin: From Middle English latent, latente, from Old French latent, from Latin latēns, present participle of lateō (“lie hidden”).

words.definition: Inactive, sleeping, asleep, suspended.
words.origin: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin dormiēns, present participle of dormiō (“to sleep”).

words.definition: Emerging; just coming into existence.
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin nāscēns, nāscentis, present participle of nāscor (“to be born”). Doublet of naissant.

words.definition: In an initial stage; beginning, starting, coming into existence.
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin incipiēns, present participle of incipiō (“begin”).

words.definition: Of or relating to an embryo.
words.origin: From New Latin embryonicus.

words.definition: Of or relating to one or more rudiments; of the nature of an early stage.
words.origin: From rudiment + -ary (adjectival suffix), perhaps after New Latin rudīmentārius, from Classical Latin rudīmentum (“first attempt; beginning”) + -ārius (adjectival suffix). Compare French rudimentaire.

words.definition: Relating to the basic, essential or fundamental part of something.
words.origin: From Middle English elementare, from Latin elementārius (“elementary”), from elementum (“one of the four elements of antiquity; fundamentals”) + -ārius (adjective-forming suffix). Cognate with French élémentaire.

words.definition: Understood by only a few.
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin arcānus (“hidden, secret”), from arceō (“to shut up, enclose”); cognate with Latin arca (“a chest”).

words.definition: Worldly, earthly, profane, vulgar as opposed to heavenly.
words.origin: From Middle English mondeyne, from Old French mondain, from Late Latin mundānus, from Latin mundus (“world”). Compare Danish mondæn.

words.definition: The condition of failing to meet an obligation.

words.definition: The condition of being insolvent; the state or condition of a person who is insolvent; the condition of being unable to pay debts as they fall due, or in the usual course of trade and business.
words.origin: From insolvent + -cy.

words.definition: A legally declared or recognized condition of insolvency of a person or organization.
words.origin: From bankrupt + -cy, replacing earlier bankruptship.

words.definition: The office and duties of a receiver.
words.origin: From receiver + -ship.

words.definition: An act, instance of, or state of expansion or increase in size, especially by injection of a gas or liquid.
words.origin: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French inflation (“swelling”), from Latin īnflātiō (“expansion", "blowing up”), from īnflātus, the perfect passive participle of īnflō (“blow into, expand”), from in (“into”) + flō (“blow”).

words.definition: An act or instance of deflating.
words.origin: From deflate + -ion.

words.definition: Prolonged high inflation accompanied by stagnant growth, often with recession and high unemployment.
words.origin: Blend of stagnation + inflation, generally thought to have been coined by the British politician Iain Macleod (1913–1970) in a 17 November 1965 parliamentary speech: see the quotation.

words.definition: The act or an instance of receding or withdrawing.
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin recessiō, from recēdō (“recede, retreat”), from re- (“back”) + cēdō (“to go”). By surface analysis, recess + -ion.

words.definition: Of, pertaining to, or consisting of money.
words.origin: From Middle French monétaire, from Late Latin monētārius (“pertaining to money”), from Latin monētārius (“of a mint”), from monēta (“mint, coinage”), from the presence—from 273 BC to AD 84—of the chief Roman mint at the Templum Iunonis…

words.definition: Related to the treasury of a country, company, region or city, particularly to government spending and revenue.
words.origin: From Middle French fiscal, from Latin fiscus (“treasury”) – see fiscus and fisc.

words.definition: A place where treasure is stored safely.
words.origin: From Middle English tresorie, from Old French tresorie, from tresor (“treasure”), from Latin thēsaurus (“treasure”), from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “treasure house”). Displaced native Old English māþmhūs.

words.definition: An obligation, debt or responsibility owed to someone.
words.origin: From liable + -ity.

words.definition: Anything that is provided or furnished by an environment to an organism dwelling within it.
words.origin: From afford + -ance; coined in 1977 by psychologist James J. Gibson, and adopted in 1988 by Donald Norman in the context of human-machine interaction.

words.definition: A body of authoritative officials organized in nested ranks.
words.origin: From Middle English ierarchie, jerarchie, from Old French ierarchie, jerarchie, from Late Latin ierarchia, from Latin hierarchia, from Ancient Greek ἱεραρχία (hierarkhía, “rule of a high priest”), from ἱεράρχης (hierárkhēs, “high priest”),…

words.definition: The art or practice of setting and arranging type; typesetting.
words.origin: From French typographie from Medieval Latin typographia from Ancient Greek τυπογράφος (tupográphos, “certified copy”) + -ίᾱ (-íā). By surface analysis, type + -o- + -graphy.

words.definition: The adjustment of the horizontal space between selected pairs of glyphs in a typeface.
words.origin: From kern (“part of a letter which extends into the space used by another letter”) + -ing, from French carne (“corner”).

words.definition: The act or process by which something is tracked.

words.definition: A line that is a base for measurement or for construction.
words.origin: From base + line.

words.definition: A rectangular array of squares or rectangles of equal size, such as in a crossword puzzle.
words.origin: Back-formation or clipping of griddle or gridiron.

words.definition: A prepared channel in a surface, especially at the side of a road adjacent to a curb, intended for the drainage of water.
words.origin: From Middle English gutter, guttur, goter, from Anglo-Norman guttere, from Old French goutiere (French gouttière), ultimately from Latin gutta (“drop”).

words.definition: The edge of the paper, typically left blank when printing but sometimes used for annotations etc.
words.origin: From Middle English margyn, from Latin marginem (possibly via Old French margin), accusative of margō (“edge, brink, border, margin”). Doublet of marge and margo.

words.definition: Alternative form of white space.
The degree of this difference.
words.origin: From French contraster, from Latin contrāstāre (“to resist", "to withstand”), from contrā (“against”) + stō, stāre (“to stand”).

words.definition: The property of being legible or easily readable.
The property of being capable of being read; legibility.
words.origin: From readable + -ity or read + -ability.

words.definition: A short line added to the end of a stroke in traditional typefaces, such as Times New Roman.

words.definition: Alternative spelling of sans serif.
A figure carved in relief or incised, especially representing a sound, word, or idea.
words.origin: First attested in 1727. Borrowed from French glyphe, from Ancient Greek γλυφή (gluphḗ, “carving”), from γλύφω (glúphō, “I carve, engrave”).

words.definition: The act of tying or binding something.
words.origin: From Middle English ligature, from Middle French ligature, from Late Latin ligātūra, from ligāre (“to tie, bind”).

words.definition: A person or thing that ascends.
words.origin: From ascend + -er.

words.definition: A person or thing that descends.
words.origin: From descend + -er (agent noun suffix).

words.definition: The distance between the baseline and midline in a typeface, typically equal to the height of the lower-case letter x.
The downwards force an object experiences due to gravity.
words.origin: From Middle English weight, weiȝte, weght, wight, from Old English wiht, ġewiht (“weight”), from Proto-Germanic *wihtiz ("weight"; compare *weganą (“to move”)), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to move; pull; draw; drive”).

words.definition: Designed to resemble a handwriting style developed in Italy in the 16th century.
words.origin: Named after the nation of Italy, as it was first used by an Italian printer, Aldo Manuzio, around 1500. Literally Italy + -ic.

words.definition: Not erect or perpendicular; not parallel to, or at right angles from, the base.
words.origin: From Middle French oblique, from Latin oblīquus (also spelled oblīcus) (“slanting, sideways, indirect, envious”).

words.definition: A thin board on which a painter lays and mixes colours.
words.origin: Borrowed from French palette. Doublet of pallet.

words.definition: A color, or shade of color; tint; dye.
words.origin: From Middle English hewe, from Old English hīew (“appearance, form, species, kind; apparition; hue, color; beauty; figure of speech”), from Proto-West Germanic *hiwi, from Proto-Germanic *hiwją (“hue, form, shape, appearance;

words.definition: The act of saturating or the process of being saturated.
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin saturatio, saturationem.

words.definition: The quality of being luminous.
A slope or incline.
words.origin: From Latin gradiēns, present participle of gradior (“to step, to walk”).

words.definition: The feel or shape of a surface or substance; the smoothness, roughness, softness, etc. of something.
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French texture, borrowed from Latin textūra (“a weaving, web, texture, structure”), from textus, past participle of texere (“to weave”). See text. Doublet of tessitura.

words.definition: The act of putting together; assembly.
words.origin: From Middle English composicioun, borrowed from Old French composicion, from Latin compositiō, compositiōnem.

words.definition: A state in which opposing forces harmonise; equilibrium.
words.origin: From Middle English balaunce, from Old French balance, from Late Latin *bilancia, from (accusative form of) Latin bilanx (“two-scaled”), from bi- + lanx (“plate, scale”).

words.definition: The variation of strong and weak elements (such as duration, accent) of sounds, notably in speech or music, over time; a beat or meter.
words.origin: First coined in 1557, from Latin rhythmus, from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός (rhuthmós, “any measured flow or movement, symmetry, rhythm”), from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow, run, stream, gush”).

words.definition: A quantity of something that is part of the whole amount or number.
words.origin: From Middle English proporcion, from Old French proportion, from Latin prōportiō (“comparative relation, proportion, symmetry, analogy”), from pro (“for, before”) + portio (“share, part”); see portion. By surface analysis, pro- + portion.

words.definition: An arrangement of items in a line.
words.origin: From French alignement, by surface analysis, align + -ment.

words.definition: Closeness; the state of being near in space, time, or relationship.
words.origin: From Middle French proximité, from Latin proximitās, proximitāt-, from proximus. By surface analysis, proxim(ate) + -ity.

words.origin: Borrowed from German Gestalt (“shape, figure, form”).

words.definition: The incorporation of obsolete or skeuomorphic elements into a design, for familiarity or out of tradition, even though they no longer serve any functional purpose.
words.origin: From Ancient Greek σκεῦος (skeûos, “implement”) + -morphism, or skeuomorph + -ism.

words.definition: A style of art that emphasises extreme simplicity of form.
words.origin: From minimal + -ism.

words.definition: Brutal, violent behaviour; savagery.
words.origin: From brutal + -ism.

words.definition: A visual model of an electronic representation of a three-dimensional object as defined geometrically by line segments.
words.origin: From wire + frame. The figurative use is extended from the literal (pre-computing and non-computing) concept of a wire frame, a frame made of wire.

words.definition: An original form or object which is a basis for other forms or objects (particularly manufactured items), or for its generalizations and models.

words.definition: Alternative form of mock-up.
words.origin: See mock-up.

words.definition: A recital or a second performance; a repetition.
words.origin: From Latin iterātiō, from iterō. Morphologically iterate + -ion.

words.definition: That employs a practical method not guaranteed to be optimal or perfect; either not following or derived from any theory, or based on an advisedly oversimplified one.
words.origin: Irregular formation from Ancient Greek εὑρίσκω (heurískō, “I find, discover”) (compare the proper Greek term εὑρετικός (heuretikós)).

words.definition: The state or condition of being usable.
words.origin: From usable + -ity or use + -ability.

words.definition: The quality of being accessible, or of admitting approach; receptiveness.
words.origin: From accessible + -ity, after Late Latin accessibilitas, from Latin accessibilis.

words.definition: A rule whereby players are only allowed to bet the money they have on the table.
Alternative form of canary in a coal mine.
Easily obtained gains; what can be obtained by readily available means.
To change a situation to a noticeable degree; to make an appreciable difference.
words.origin: From the indicator needle of a measuring instrument such as a speedometer, dial indicator, etc; used both literally and figuratively.

words.definition: To undertake an overwhelmingly difficult task or approach to a problem.
A radical change in thinking from an accepted point of view to a new one, necessitated when new scientific discoveries produce anomalies in the current paradigm.
words.origin: Coined by American historian, physicist and philosopher Thomas Kuhn in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962).

words.definition: A benefit that is also a liability, especially a benefit that carries some significant but not-so-obvious cost or risk.
words.origin: From the notion that if two sides of the same blade are sharp, it cuts both ways. The metaphor may have originated from the Arabic expression سَيْفٌ ذُو حَدَّيْنِ (sayfun ḏū ḥaddayni, “double-edged sword”) or from the Hebrew expression חֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת…

words.definition: A problem or difficult issue that is very obvious, but is ignored for the convenience or comfort of those involved.
words.origin: Likely US origin, or possibly from Ivan Andreyevich Krylov's 1814 fable, The Inquisitive Man, which tells of a man going to a museum and noticing all sorts of things apart from an elephant.

words.definition: A herring that is cured in smoke and brine strong enough to turn the flesh red; a type of kipper.

words.definition: One who debates from a viewpoint which one may not actually hold, usually to determine its validity or simply for the sake of argument.
words.origin: Calque of Latin advocātus diabolī (“the devil’s advocate”), a popular title given to the officer dealing with the canonization process in the 16th c.

words.definition: A general guideline, rather than a strict rule; an approximate measure or means of reckoning based on experience or common knowledge.
words.origin: Attested since 1658. Of uncertain origin, but probably based on the use of the thumb as reference for various measurements.

words.definition: A small indication of a larger possibility; the first part encountered of a problem that is much bigger than it seems.

words.definition: Indicates that one must try a different strategy in order to achieve some goal following the failure of a recent attempt.
words.origin: Coined as “Well, back to the old drawing board,” as the caption of a cartoon by Peter Arno of The New Yorker on March 1, 1941, depicting a delighted engineer walking away from a crashed plane.

words.definition: In broad agreement or sharing a common general understanding or knowledge (common in office environments).
To begin; to start some action; to set in motion.
To begin an activity immediately and with full commitment.
To quit; to give up.
words.origin: From the traditional signal from a boxer's support staff of throwing such an item into a boxing ring to indicate that the contestant cannot continue the match and is forfeiting to the opponent.

Not yet resolved, finished, answered, decided or certain.
Scheduled to occur in the future.
Informed; up to date; having current knowledge; part of the discussion.
Not informed, up-to-date, or current; not included in a process or discussion.
words.origin: First use appears c. 1973. See cite below. Its use is thought by some to have roots in computer or telephony terminology.

words.definition: To accept a negative aspect of a situation in order to proceed.
words.origin: Possibly from the reported practice of soldiers biting a bullet to avoid crying out in pain, usually during a medical procedure or punishment. See the Wikipedia article Bite the bullet for a further discussion of possible etymologies.

words.definition: To work studiously, especially late into the night.
words.origin: Originally referring to the act of burning lamp oil in oil lamps for light at night. The collocation midnight oil in its literal sense is attested from mid 17th c.

words.definition: To cease an activity.
words.origin: From earlier call it half a day, which first appears c. 1834, meaning to leave before the working day was over.

words.definition: To make an extra effort; to do a particularly good job.
words.origin: * Possibly from the gospel of Matthew ch.5: v.41 *: "And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain."

words.definition: To put forth great effort to meet requirements, usually arbitrary, set by someone.
words.origin: Reminiscent of a circus animal performing tricks by jumping through hoops.

words.definition: To learn the basics or master introductory knowledge.
words.origin: Of nautical origin: in the past, the phrase “he knows the ropes” written on a seaman’s discharge meant that he was inexperienced and familiar only with a ship’s principal ropes.

words.definition: To fail to take advantage of an opportunity; to overlook or be too late to pursue an option or course of action.
words.origin: Allusion to failing to catch a boat in time, effectively “missing” the boat. Popular since the 1920s.

words.origin: See blue moon. First use appears c. 1833. See citation below.

words.definition: To unplug or cut power to a machine.
To raise standards or expectations, especially by creating something to a higher standard.
To infer a meaning that is not stated explicitly.
words.origin: Probably from glosses and commentaries which were written between the lines and provided the reader with additional information not explicitly stated in the text.

words.definition: To agree, especially in every respect; to concur; to get along.
To remain neutral on a certain topic, to not have a stance or opinion.
Without attracting notice; in an undetected or secretive manner.

words.origin: Possibly calque of Danish kvantespring.

words.origin: After Greek king Pyrrhus of Epirus, who suffered heavy losses while defeating the Romans.

words.definition: A difficult situation from which there is no escape because it involves mutually conflicting or dependent conditions.
words.origin: Coined by American writer Joseph Heller in 1961 in his novel Catch-22, in which the main character feigns madness in order to avoid dangerous combat missions, but his desire to avoid them is taken to prove his sanity.

words.definition: The state of things; the way things are, as opposed to the way they could be; the existing state of affairs.
words.origin: From Latin status (“state”) (sometimes used in the ablative statū) + quō (“in which”), the ablative of quī (“which”).

words.definition: Something which is understood as something else; an equivocation.
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin quid prō quō (literally “something for something”).

words.definition: For a particular purpose.
words.origin: Learned borrowing from New Latin ad hoc (“to this, for this”).

words.definition: In actual use or existence, regardless of official or legal status.
words.origin: Unadapted borrowing from Latin dē factō (literally “according to fact”), from dē (“according to”) + ablative of factum (“fact, deed, act”).

words.definition: Without determination by or involvement of extraneous factors; by its very nature.
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin per sē (“by itself”), from per (“by, through”) and sē (“itself, himself, herself, themselves”).
